projectTitle: Fernbridge Logistics: Real-Time Package Visibility, Start to Finish
projectTagline: A 20-video, start-to-finish build of a medallion lakehouse and a real-time status feed — Azure Databricks, Delta Lake, Kafka, and Microsoft Fabric, for one fictional regional parcel carrier, from a day-stale CSV export to a live "where's my package" answer.
businessContext:
**Fernbridge Logistics** is a fictional regional parcel delivery company: roughly 200 delivery vehicles across a 6-state Southeast footprint, each with a handheld scanner and a GPS tracker, moving about 82,000 packages a day. Scan and GPS events stream constantly, but nobody has ever built a real data platform for them — an Operations analyst pulls a batch CSV export by hand into Excel once a day for trend reporting, and customer-support reps answering "where's my package" calls can only see yesterday's status, because there is no real-time visibility into anything.

You've been brought in as a Data Engineer to fix both problems at once: a proper historical lakehouse for Operations' trend analytics, and a near-real-time package-status feed Support can actually trust. This series follows that build end to end — including a real production bug that briefly showed a delivered package as still out for delivery, found, root-caused, and fixed in front of the people it affected.
architectureSummary: By the end of this series, Fernbridge Logistics has: all infrastructure (Databricks workspace, ADLS Gen2 storage, Fabric capacity, networking) provisioned through Terraform and Bicep, version-controlled and CI-tested, never clicked together by hand; a Kafka topic (`fernbridge.delivery-events`, partitioned by vehicle for per-vehicle ordering) carrying every scan and GPS event; a medallion lakehouse on Azure Databricks and Delta Lake — Bronze (raw, append-only), Silver (deduplicated, conformed), and Gold (`package_status_gold`, `delivery_performance_gold`) — resolving one governed current status per package; and two deliberately separate Microsoft Fabric consumption surfaces: a Power BI-style report on the Gold tables for Operations' trend analytics, and a real-time Eventhouse/KQL feed, read independently from the same Kafka topic, for Support's live lookups. A real out-of-order-arrival bug that briefly reverted a delivered package's status was found, root-caused, fixed, and covered by a permanent regression test. Nothing here is more advanced than the tools taught earlier in this path — the point of this series is showing how Databricks, Delta Lake, Kafka, Fabric, Terraform/Bicep, and Git/CI fit together on one real job, not introducing new tools.

lessons.title: Meeting Fernbridge: Why Support Can't Answer 'Where's My Package'
lessons.summary: The discovery meeting: uncovering why Fernbridge Logistics has a day-old trend report and a support desk that can't see today's package status, before any pipeline gets designed.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
Over the next 20 videos, you'll build a real data platform for a fictional regional parcel carrier, **Fernbridge Logistics** — roughly 200 delivery vehicles running routes across a six-state Southeast footprint (Georgia, South Carolina, North Carolina, Tennessee, Alabama, and Florida), scanning somewhere around 82,000 packages a day. Every one of those vehicles already carries a handheld scanner and a GPS tracker, and both devices are already generating a constant stream of events — a scan every time a package is picked up, loaded out for delivery, delivered, or flagged as an exception, and a GPS ping roughly every 45 seconds while a route is active. None of that data has ever had anywhere real to go.

By the end of this series you'll have a Kafka event stream, a medallion lakehouse on Azure Databricks and Delta Lake, and two very different Microsoft Fabric consumption surfaces built on top of it — all provisioned through Terraform and Bicep, tested through Git CI. This video starts where a project like this always starts: not with a line of infrastructure code, but with a discovery meeting where two people who both agree something is badly broken turn out to be describing two different problems.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine your school bus has a GPS on it the whole time, so it technically always knows exactly where it is. But the school office only ever looks at that GPS once, at the very end of the day, and writes down one single sentence in a notebook: "the bus finished its route." So if your mom calls the school at 3pm asking where the bus is right now, the office has nothing to tell her — not because the bus doesn't know where it is, but because nobody ever built a way to ask it in the moment.

That is exactly what is happening at Fernbridge Logistics. Every scanner and every GPS tracker on every truck already knows what is happening right now. But the only thing anyone ever does with that information is print one big spreadsheet once a day, after the fact. So when a customer calls asking where their package actually is today, the people answering the phones are stuck looking at yesterday's notebook, same as that confused school office.
lessons.explainProfessional:
This is the discovery phase of a data engineering engagement, and the pattern you'll see here recurs constantly in the real world: the telemetry already exists at the edge — the handheld scanner and the GPS tracker are both generating events continuously — but no platform has ever been built to capture, store, or serve any of it centrally. What looks like a single complaint ("our data is bad") is almost always two distinct, differently-shaped problems wearing the same complaint, and your job in this first meeting is to tell them apart before anyone starts drawing an architecture diagram.

At Fernbridge, you'll hear both problems in the same room, from two different stakeholders, within the first ten minutes. Renata Ocampo, the VP of Operations, is frustrated that her team's trend reporting is built on a manual CSV export that's already a day stale before anyone opens it — a **historical/analytical** gap: the data eventually exists correctly, it just arrives too slowly and requires a person in the loop every single morning. Devon Marsh, the Director of Customer Support, has a completely different complaint: his reps can't tell a customer where a package is *right now*, because there is no current-state view at all — a **real-time/operational** gap, where the problem isn't staleness, it's that no system has ever been built to answer "what is true at this exact moment." Those two gaps get solved by genuinely different architecture later in this series — a batch lakehouse for one, an event-streaming path for the other — which is exactly why naming them as two separate problems, out loud, in this first meeting, matters more than it sounds like it should.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 — Walk in already knowing the telemetry exists

Before the meeting, write down the one fact that reframes everything: Fernbridge isn't missing data at the source. Every one of its roughly 200 vehicles already carries a handheld scanner (firing a scan event on pickup, out-for-delivery, delivery, and exception) and a GPS tracker (pinging location roughly every 45 seconds on an active route, adding up to something like 160,000 location pings a day fleet-wide). The problem can't be "we need to start collecting data" — it's "nothing has ever been built to capture, store, or serve what's already being generated."

## Step 2 — Interview Operations and Support separately

```
RENATA: Every morning, Felix pulls a CSV export out of the scanner
        vendor's portal by hand and drops it into Excel. It takes him
        about ninety minutes, and by the time the regional directors
        open the trend deck, we're already looking at yesterday's
        numbers to make today's decisions. We scan about 82,000
        packages a day across six states -- and our "analytics" is
        one person and a spreadsheet.

DEVON:  My team fields around 310 "where's my package" calls a day.
        About a third of those -- call it 100 a day -- end with a rep
        telling the customer "let me call you back," because the only
        status on screen is whatever the scanner showed as of
        yesterday's batch. The package could have been delivered an
        hour ago and we'd have no idea.
```

Felix Tran, Renata's Senior Operations Analyst, confirms the manual pull directly: "I open the vendor portal at 6am, export, clean it up, and load it into the shared workbook. If I'm out sick, the trend report just doesn't happen that day."

## Step 3 — Name the two problems out loud, separately, in the room

```
YOU:    Renata, if the CSV arrived perfectly on time every morning,
        would that fix Devon's problem too?
RENATA: No -- it would still only be a snapshot from this morning.
        Devon needs to know what's happening *right now*, during
        the day. That's not the same ask as my trend reporting at all.
DEVON:  Exactly. I don't need better history. I need to know where a
        package is the moment a customer calls.
```

That exchange is the whole discovery in miniature: one organization, one bad complaint ("our data is late"), two genuinely different engineering problems underneath it.

## Step 4 — Write the one-page current-state artifact

```
FERNBRIDGE LOGISTICS -- CURRENT STATE AUDIT

Telemetry source:   200 vehicles, handheld scanner + GPS tracker each.
                     Already generating scan + location events
                     continuously. Nothing captures them centrally.

Gap 1 (Operations):  Historical/analytical. Daily CSV export, manual,
                      ~90 min, done by one analyst (Felix). Trend
                      reports are a day stale before anyone reads them.

Gap 2 (Support):      Real-time/operational. No current-state view
                      exists at all. ~310 contacts/day, ~100/day end
                      in a callback because status is stale.

Agreement so far: these are TWO problems, not one. Gap 1 needs a
reliable, automated historical pipeline. Gap 2 needs a near-real-time
status feed. Neither has been scoped yet -- that's Lesson 2 and 3.
```

## Step 5 — Separate "broken" from "never built"

Neither gap is a bug. The manual CSV process isn't malfunctioning — it's doing exactly what a human-run, once-a-day export can do. The support desk's stale view isn't a defect in the scanner — no real-time path from scanner to support screen has ever existed. Logging that distinction now keeps the next two lessons focused on building the right thing, instead of "fixing" a system that was never designed to do what everyone now needs from it.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Ran discovery with Operations (Renata Ocampo) and Support (Devon Marsh). Telemetry already exists at the edge -- scanners and GPS trackers on all ~200 vehicles fire continuously -- but nothing captures it centrally. Two distinct gaps surfaced: a historical/analytical one (manual daily CSV export, ~90 min, a day stale) and a real-time/operational one (no current-state view exists for support at all). These need different architecture downstream and shouldn't be conflated into one fix.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: We met with Operations and Support and documented, in their own words and with real numbers, why Fernbridge's reporting is slow and why support reps can't answer basic status questions. These turned out to be two separate problems wearing one complaint, which is the single most important thing we learned before any design work starts.
workplaceExplanation.executive: We now understand precisely why your trend reports lag and why support can't answer a simple "where's my package" question -- it's not one broken system, it's two gaps that have simply never been built: a slow manual reporting process, and a real-time view that's never existed. We have that documented, which is what lets us fix both the right way instead of patching one and leaving the other.

lessons.title: Turning 'We Need Real-Time Visibility' Into a Testable Requirement
lessons.summary: Converting Devon's vague 'support needs real-time visibility' into a precise, testable latency and data requirement before any pipeline design begins.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
Lesson 1 named two separate problems at Fernbridge: a historical reporting gap and a real-time status gap. That's enough to understand the shape of the project, but "support needs real-time visibility" is not something you can build against yet — it's a feeling, not a specification. This video turns that feeling into a written, testable requirement: an exact definition of what "current status" means, how fresh it has to be, which events decide it, and what happens on the edge cases that will absolutely show up in production, like two events arriving out of order.

This requirement is what every later architecture decision in this series answers to — the Kafka topic design, the Silver-layer conformance logic, the Fabric real-time surface, and eventually the real duplicate-delivery bug this project hits and fixes, all trace back to the exact definition you're about to pin down with Devon and Renata in this room.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine you tell a friend "text me back quickly" and leave it at that. One friend thinks quickly means within a minute, another thinks it means sometime today. You'll both be upset with each other, and neither of you did anything wrong — you just never agreed on what "quickly" actually meant in minutes.

That's exactly the trap hiding inside "support needs real-time visibility." Everyone nods in the meeting because it sounds obviously true, but nobody has actually said how many seconds or minutes is good enough, or what happens if two updates about the same package show up in the wrong order. This video is where we turn that fuzzy wish into an exact, written rule specific enough that we could later build a test to check whether the system is actually meeting it.
lessons.explainProfessional:
A requirement that sounds reasonable in a meeting and a requirement you can actually architect against are two different documents, and most streaming projects quietly fail in that gap. The discipline is to make every clause falsifiable: given a specific scan event at a specific timestamp, there has to be an unambiguous, checkable answer for what a support rep's screen should show and by when. "Real-time" is not implementable. "A scan event reaching the Kafka topic must be reflected in the support-facing status view within 2 minutes, and the status shown must always be the event with the latest true event timestamp for that package, not simply the most recently received event" is implementable, and just as importantly, it's something Devon and Renata can each immediately agree or disagree with.

That last clause — latest *event* timestamp, not latest *received* timestamp — is the one worth getting exactly right in this meeting, because out-of-order delivery is a real property of distributed event systems, not a hypothetical. A GPS tracker or handheld scanner that briefly loses signal can transmit a backlog of events the moment it reconnects, and those events can easily arrive at the Kafka topic in a different order than they actually happened on the truck. If the requirement is written sloppily as "show whatever update came in last," the system will faithfully implement a bug — and this exact gap is what reappears, deliberately, as the duplicate-delivery incident later in this series. Pinning the rule down now, in writing, with both stakeholders' sign-off, is what makes that later debugging episode traceable back to a spec instead of a guess.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 — Pull the testable claims out of Lesson 1's audit

```
FROM THE AUDIT:
  - Support needs a "current status" view -- but "current" and
    "real-time" were never defined in seconds or minutes
  - Events can arrive out of order (a tracker reconnecting after a
    signal gap is a normal, expected occurrence, not an edge case)
  - Operations' trend reporting can tolerate next-day data -- that's
    a DIFFERENT freshness requirement than Support's, and conflating
    them risks over-building one and under-building the other
```

## Step 2 — Draft the candidate requirement and pressure-test it live

```
DRAFT REQUIREMENT v1:
"A scan or GPS event reaching the Kafka topic must be reflected in the
support-facing package status within 2 minutes. The status shown for
a package must always be derived from the event with the latest TRUE
EVENT TIMESTAMP for that package, never simply the most recently
RECEIVED event."
```

```
DEVON:  Two minutes is fine -- honestly even five would beat what we
        have today, which is a full day.
YOU:    Good, so 2 minutes is the target, not the minimum we need.
        Now -- if a truck loses signal for ten minutes and then sends
        three backed-up scan events all at once, which one should a
        rep see?
DEVON:  Whichever one actually happened last on the truck. Not
        whichever one happens to arrive at our system last.
RENATA: And for my trend reports, I genuinely don't care about any
        of this -- next-day is fine for me, it always has been. Don't
        build me a 2-minute pipeline, that's solving a problem I
        don't have.
```

That last line from Renata is important: it confirms the two freshness requirements are legitimately different and shouldn't be merged into one over-engineered pipeline.

## Step 3 — Write the requirement with a concrete verification example

```
REQUIREMENT (v1, support-facing status):
  Latency: scan/GPS event -> visible support status, within 2 minutes.
  Ordering: status reflects the event with the latest EVENT_TIMESTAMP
            (when it happened on the device), never latest
            INGESTION_TIMESTAMP (when it arrived at the platform).
  Verification example:
    Event A: package 10045, OUT_FOR_DELIVERY, event_timestamp 2:00pm,
             arrives at 2:01pm (signal was fine)
    Event B: package 10045, DELIVERED, event_timestamp 1:58pm,
             arrives at 2:04pm (was stuck in a 6-minute signal gap)
    Correct displayed status at 2:05pm: OUT_FOR_DELIVERY (event A's
    2:00pm timestamp is later than event B's 1:58pm timestamp, even
    though B is a "later" status type and arrived more recently).

REQUIREMENT (v1, operations trend reporting):
  Latency: full prior day's data available by 7:00am next day.
  Ordering: not latency-sensitive; a nightly batch resolving final
            state per package is sufficient.
```

## Step 4 — Review line by line, get an explicit yes from both stakeholders

Read the ordering rule aloud to Devon specifically, since it's the one most likely to get hand-waved past: "if two updates disagree, we always trust whichever one actually happened earlier or later in the real world, not whichever one showed up first in our system." Get an explicit yes, not a nod — this exact sentence becomes the acceptance criterion for the Silver-layer logic you'll build many lessons from now.

## Step 5 — Version and date the requirement

Save it as `Fernbridge_Status_Visibility_Requirement_v1.md`, dated and signed by Renata and Devon. Lesson 3 uses this document, alongside the current-state audit, to draw the actual v1 scope line.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Converted "support needs real-time visibility" into a written requirement: 2-minute latency from event to visible status, with status always resolved by the event's true timestamp rather than its arrival order at the platform. Confirmed Operations' trend reporting has a genuinely different, much looser freshness requirement (next-day by 7am), so the two don't get collapsed into one over-built pipeline.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: We now have a specific, numbers-based definition of what 'real-time' actually means for Support, separate from a much looser, already-sufficient definition for Operations' reporting. That gives us a concrete target to design against instead of an open-ended goal that could keep expanding.
workplaceExplanation.executive: We've turned a vague request for 'real-time visibility' into an exact, agreed-upon target -- status visible within two minutes, always reflecting what truly happened first. That's what lets us build the right-sized system instead of guessing at how fast is fast enough.

lessons.title: Scoping V1: Batch Lakehouse Now, Real-Time Status Next
lessons.summary: Drawing a hard written line around what ships first -- the historical lakehouse for Operations -- and what's explicitly sequenced next rather than built simultaneously.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
You now have two written, signed-off requirements: a 2-minute real-time status target for Support, and a next-day-by-7am target for Operations' trend reporting. That's enough to plan against — but not enough to start building, because both requirements landing on one data engineer's desk at the same time creates real pressure to build everything at once. This video draws the hard scope line for v1: the governed historical lakehouse ships first, built on Kafka, Databricks, and Delta Lake, and the real-time Fabric Eventhouse feed for Support is explicitly sequenced second, not dropped and not built in parallel.

This isn't just a scheduling preference. The real-time feed in v2 depends directly on the conformed, deduplicated Silver-layer events this v1 lakehouse establishes — building the real-time piece first, on top of unvalidated event logic, is exactly how you'd end up debugging a duplicate-status bug with no foundation underneath it to trust.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine you're asked to build a treehouse with a rope swing attached to it. You could try to hang the rope swing and build the treehouse platform at the exact same time, but then you'd be tying a swing to boards that might not even be sturdy yet. The smarter order is to build the solid platform first, test that it holds weight, and then hang the swing from something you already know is safe.

That's exactly the plan here. The "platform" is a reliable system that correctly captures and cleans up every scan and GPS event. The "rope swing" is the fast, real-time screen support reps will use. We're building the platform first, proving it gets events right, and only then hanging the real-time swing off of it -- instead of building both at once and hoping they both turn out sturdy.
lessons.explainProfessional:
This is scope sequencing applied to a problem with two genuinely different stakeholders and two genuinely different latency requirements, and the trap to avoid is treating both as equally urgent just because both surfaced in the same discovery week. They are not architecturally independent: the real-time support feed needs clean, deduplicated, correctly-ordered delivery events to serve a trustworthy status, and that cleanup logic is exactly what the batch lakehouse's Bronze-to-Silver conformance step is going to build and prove out first. Building the real-time path before that conformance logic exists means debugging event ordering and deduplication live, in a latency-sensitive system, with Support already depending on it — a much worse place to find that kind of bug than inside a batch pipeline with room to inspect and fix it.

The v1 boundary for Fernbridge is therefore structural, not arbitrary: Bronze ingestion of the raw Kafka stream, a Silver layer that resolves exactly the ordering and deduplication questions pinned down in Lesson 2, two Gold tables (`package_status_gold` and `delivery_performance_gold`), and a Fabric/Power BI report for Operations' trend analytics. The Fabric Eventhouse real-time surface for Support — which this whole 20-video arc is building toward — is deferred to v2, not because it's less important, but because it is safer and faster to build on top of Silver-layer logic that's already been validated against real data, rather than racing to build it blind. Naming that sequencing reason explicitly, out loud, is what keeps Devon from reasonably asking why his higher-visibility, more time-sensitive problem isn't going first.


## Step 2 — Give each item an explicit, honest disposition

```
ITEM                              DISPOSITION      WHY
Bronze/Silver/Gold lakehouse       Included in v1   Structural -- every
  (historical, Operations)                           other item depends on
                                                      clean, conformed
                                                      events existing first.
Real-time status feed (Support)    Sequenced next    Depends directly on
                                    (v2, this same    the Silver-layer
                                    engagement)        ordering/dedup logic
                                                      v1 builds and proves.

                                                      top of a proven

```

## Step 3 — Write the v1 scope statement plainly

```
FERNBRIDGE DATA PLATFORM -- V1 SCOPE

Ships in v1:
  - Kafka ingestion of scan + GPS events (fernbridge.delivery-events)
  - Bronze: raw events landed as-is, append-only
  - Silver: cleaned, deduplicated, correctly-ordered delivery events
  - Gold: package_status_gold, delivery_performance_gold
  - Fabric/Power BI report on Gold for Operations' trend analytics
  - All infrastructure provisioned via Terraform/Bicep, tested via CI

Sequenced immediately after (v2, same engagement, not a separate ask):
  - Fabric Eventhouse/KQL real-time surface for Support's 2-minute
    status requirement, built directly on the v1 Silver layer

Explicitly deferred, logged, not forgotten:
  - Predictive ETA, driver scorecards, public tracking page,
    route optimization
```

## Step 4 — Rehearse the scope-creep conversation before it happens mid-build

```
DEVON:  My problem is the urgent one -- customers are calling today.
        Why does Operations' report go first?
YOU:    Because the real-time feed you need has to be built on top of
        events that are already cleaned up and deduplicated -- and
        that cleanup is exactly what the lakehouse build proves out.
        Building your feed first means debugging duplicate or
        out-of-order events live, in the system reps are already
        relying on. Building it second means it inherits logic we've
        already tested. You get a more reliable result faster this
        way, not a slower one.
```

## Step 5 — Get written sign-off on the boundary and the sequence

Attach this scope statement to both signed requirement documents from Lessons 1 and 2, and get explicit confirmation from Renata and Devon on the sequence specifically — not just the feature list. The sequence is the part most likely to be challenged later, so it needs the same explicit sign-off as the scope itself.

## Step 6 — Write down the dependency, not just the order

It's not enough to say the lakehouse ships "first" — write down specifically *why* v2 depends on it, so the reasoning survives even if someone other than you picks up v2 later:

```
DEPENDENCY NOTE (for anyone picking up v2):
  The Eventhouse real-time feed reads conformed events, not raw Kafka
  messages. It depends on v1's Silver layer already having resolved:
    1. Deduplication (an event replayed or retried doesn't double-count)
    2. True ordering by event_timestamp, not ingestion_timestamp
       (per the Lesson 2 requirement)
  Building the real-time feed against raw Bronze data instead of
  validated Silver data would re-expose both problems directly to
  Support, in a live system, instead of catching them in a batch
  pipeline with room to inspect and fix.
```

This note is what turns "batch now, real-time next" from a scheduling preference into an engineering argument anyone on the team can verify.

Predictive ETA, driver scorecards, a public tracking page, and route optimization are all logged as deferred, not dropped.

That gives us a fast, defensible answer when Support understandably asks why their higher-visibility problem isn't first.
workplaceExplanation.executive: We agreed on exactly what ships first -- a reliable historical foundation -- and exactly what comes right after it -- the real-time status feed your support team needs. The order isn't about priority, it's about building the fast, customer-facing piece on top of logic we've already proven works.

lessons.title: Choosing the Stack: Databricks, Fabric, and Kafka, Not One Bigger Warehouse
lessons.summary: The first architecture decision: why a Kafka-plus-medallion-lakehouse-plus-dual-Fabric-surface design solves this, and why one bigger warehouse or a single Fabric Eventhouse cannot.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
With v1 scoped, this is the first real architecture decision: what actually gets built, and in which tool. The tempting shortcut is to treat this as one bigger reporting problem and just stand up a larger, faster data warehouse to replace the manual CSV export. This video walks through why that single-warehouse approach cannot satisfy both requirements pinned down in Lessons 2 and 3 at once, and why the right answer is a deliberately layered stack — Kafka for the event stream, a medallion lakehouse on Azure Databricks and Delta Lake for governed historical truth, and two different Microsoft Fabric consumption surfaces built on top of it for two genuinely different audiences.

This decision is the architectural spine the rest of this series builds on, piece by piece: the Kafka topic design, the Bronze/Silver/Gold notebooks, the Terraform and Bicep that provision all of it, and eventually the Fabric Eventhouse real-time surface all trace back to the stack chosen in this lesson.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine you need both a photo album to look back at old birthday parties and a live video call to talk to your grandma right now. You wouldn't try to use the same photo album for both jobs -- flipping pages is great for looking back, but useless for talking to someone live, and a video call screen is terrible for storing ten years of birthday photos. You'd use the right tool for each job, even though both jobs involve "seeing people."

That's exactly the choice at Fernbridge. One job is looking back at yesterday's and last month's deliveries to spot trends -- that's the photo album, and a historical lakehouse is built for exactly that. The other job is seeing a package's status right now, this second -- that's the live video call, and a real-time event system is built for exactly that. Trying to force one tool to do both jobs means it ends up doing neither one well.
lessons.explainProfessional:
A single bigger warehouse would technically let Fernbridge load more data faster than today's manual CSV process, but it solves exactly one of the two requirements from Lessons 2 and 3 — Operations' next-day trend reporting — and does nothing for Support's 2-minute status requirement, because a warehouse optimized for batch analytical queries is not built to serve a sub-second point lookup against a continuously arriving event stream. Conversely, building everything on a single real-time event store and skipping the batch lakehouse entirely would satisfy Support but leave Operations without the governed, auditable, cheaply-queryable historical layer that daily trend analytics and eventual regulatory or financial reporting depend on. Each requirement genuinely needs a different kind of engine underneath it.

That's why the right fix is a layered stack where each piece has exactly one job. Apache Kafka (topic `fernbridge.delivery-events`) decouples the handheld scanners and GPS trackers from everything downstream — it's the one place both consumers (the batch lakehouse and the eventual real-time surface) read from, so neither depends on the other's pace. Azure Databricks and Delta Lake provide the medallion lakehouse — Bronze landing the raw stream untouched, Silver resolving the ordering and deduplication logic from Lesson 2, Gold producing `package_status_gold` and `delivery_performance_gold` as the governed, queryable historical truth. Microsoft Fabric then provides two separate consumption surfaces on purpose: a Power BI report on the Gold Delta tables for Operations' trend analytics, and — built next in this series, on top of the same validated Silver stream — an Eventhouse/KQL database tuned specifically for low-latency point lookups, which is what Support's 2-minute requirement actually needs. All of it gets provisioned through Terraform and Bicep and tested through Git CI, so the infrastructure and the transformation logic are both reviewable and reproducible, not clicked together by hand.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 — List the actual constraints before naming a tool

```
CONSTRAINTS:
  - Two requirements with genuinely different latency needs: next-day
    by 7am (Operations) and 2 minutes (Support) -- one engine serving
    both well is unlikely
  - Events can arrive out of order -- whatever stores the raw stream
    needs to preserve true event order information, not just
    whichever record arrived first
  - v1 must not require replacing the handheld scanners or GPS
    trackers -- they already work and stream correctly
  - Everything must be provisioned as code and tested in CI, per the
    engagement's standing engineering practice
```

## Step 2 — Assign one layer per responsibility

```
LAYER                 TOOL             RESPONSIBLE FOR            NOT RESPONSIBLE FOR
Event ingestion        Kafka            Decoupling scanners/GPS     Storing history,
                       (fernbridge.      trackers from every         serving analytics
                       delivery-events)  downstream consumer         queries
Historical lakehouse   Databricks +     Bronze/Silver/Gold:         Sub-2-minute point
                       Delta Lake        governed, deduplicated,     lookups
                                         queryable history
Historical reporting   Fabric/Power BI  Operations' trend           Live status lookups
                       on Gold           analytics
Real-time status       Fabric           Low-latency point lookup    Long-term historical
                       Eventhouse/KQL    for Support (built next)    storage or trend
                       (v2)                                         analytics
Infrastructure          Terraform +      Reviewable, repeatable      Business logic itself
                       Bicep             provisioning
Quality gate            Git + GitHub CI  Testing infra plans and     Running the
                                         PySpark notebooks on         warehouse/stream
                                         every pull request           itself
```

## Step 3 — Name the alternatives seriously considered, and why each loses

```
- One bigger traditional data warehouse, replacing the manual CSV
  with a faster automated load: rejected as the FULL solution. It
  solves Operations' freshness problem but has no mechanism for
  Support's 2-minute requirement at all -- it's not built for
  point lookups against a live stream.
- Fabric Eventhouse for everything, including long-term historical
  trend analytics: rejected. Eventhouse is excellent for the
  low-latency lookup Support needs, but it's not the right engine
  for governed, cost-efficient, long-retention historical storage
  and the kind of deep trend analysis Operations runs monthly.
- Skipping Kafka and having the scanner vendor's system write
  directly into Databricks on a schedule: rejected. That re-creates
  the batch-only gap from Lesson 1 and gives the eventual real-time
  surface nothing live to read from.
```

## Step 4 — Write the one-paragraph justification you'll reuse later

```
"We're not replacing your scanners or GPS trackers -- they already
work. We're adding a Kafka stream so both the historical lakehouse
and the future real-time feed can read the same events independently,
a governed Databricks/Delta lakehouse for trustworthy history, and two
separate Fabric surfaces -- a Power BI report for trends, and later an
Eventhouse feed for live status -- because those are genuinely
different jobs that deserve different tools."
```

## Step 5 — Write down what this choice does NOT require

```
THIS DECISION DOES NOT REQUIRE:
  - Replacing any handheld scanner or GPS tracker hardware
  - Any change to how drivers do their jobs day to day
  - Downtime for the existing scanner vendor portal during the build
  - A single "rip and replace" cutover -- the CSV export can keep
    running in parallel until the new Gold tables are validated
```

Saying plainly what stays untouched is usually what turns a cautious stakeholder's hesitation into approval -- the real worry behind "why do we need three new tools" is almost always about risk to what already works, not the tool count itself.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Locked the architecture: Kafka topic fernbridge.delivery-events decouples scanners/GPS trackers from everything downstream, Databricks and Delta Lake own the Bronze/Silver/Gold medallion lakehouse, and Fabric provides two separate consumption surfaces -- Power BI on Gold for trend analytics now, Eventhouse/KQL for real-time status next -- because one engine can't serve both a next-day batch requirement and a 2-minute lookup requirement well. Terraform and Bicep provision all of it, tested through Git CI.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: We're not forcing one tool to do two very different jobs. Historical trend reporting and real-time status lookups have different speed requirements, so we're using a layered stack where each piece does the one thing it's actually good at, instead of a single bigger system that would end up doing both jobs poorly.
workplaceExplanation.executive: We're not replacing your scanners or trucks' GPS trackers, and we're not forcing one system to try to do two very different jobs. We're adding a stream, a governed historical platform, and two purpose-built reporting surfaces -- one for trends, one for live status -- so each actually works well instead of compromising on both.

lessons.title: Designing the Medallion Architecture: Bronze, Silver, Gold
lessons.summary: Whiteboarding Bronze, Silver, and Gold on Delta Lake -- grain, what lives in each layer, and the one place "package status" gets defined -- before opening Databricks.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
With Azure Databricks + Delta Lake, Microsoft Fabric, and Kafka chosen as the stack in the last video, this is the first real architecture decision inside Databricks itself: how the project's tables are layered. We're whiteboarding three layers -- **Bronze** (raw Kafka scan and GPS events, landed exactly as they arrived, append-only, never edited), **Silver** (cleaned, deduplicated, conformed events that both agree with each other and with the dimension data), and **Gold** (the two tables every team actually queries: `package_status_gold`, the one governed definition of "where is this package right now," and `delivery_performance_gold`, daily operational aggregates) -- before writing a single `CREATE TABLE` statement.

This layering is the architectural core of the entire Fernbridge build. Every later lesson in this series -- the Kafka ingestion path, the infrastructure that gets provisioned, and a real production bug involving duplicate "delivered" rows later in the project -- happens inside the shape drawn on this whiteboard. Get the boundary between "land it" and "decide what it means" wrong here, and support reps are right back to trusting a number nobody can fully explain, just now sitting in Delta Lake instead of a spreadsheet.
lessons.explainSimple:
Picture a loading dock behind a delivery depot. Every truck that pulls up gets unloaded onto the dock exactly as it arrives -- boxes still taped shut, nothing opened, nothing checked. Nobody throws anything away at the dock, even a box that looks damaged, because the dock's only job is to prove what actually showed up.

From there, workers move boxes into a sorting room. This is where they open things up, throw out an accidental duplicate shipment, fix a label that got smudged, and make sure every box matches the same system of names. Finally, the clean, sorted boxes go up to the front desk, where there's exactly one whiteboard that says where every package actually is right now -- not three different guesses from three different people. That's Bronze, Silver, and Gold: the loading dock, the sorting room, and the one trusted front-desk board.
lessons.explainProfessional:
This is the medallion architecture, and the discipline that matters is keeping each layer honest about exactly one job. **Bronze** is the system of record for "what did the Kafka topic actually say" -- it is append-only and immutable by design: every scan and GPS event from `fernbridge.delivery-events` lands here with its original Kafka metadata (partition, offset, event timestamp) intact, with no deduplication, no type coercion beyond what's needed to store the bytes, and absolutely no filtering. If a scanner at a depot sends the same event twice because of a network retry, Bronze keeps both rows -- that's not a bug in Bronze, that's Bronze doing its one job, which is being a faithful, replayable copy of the stream. A Bronze table you can't reprocess from scratch isn't really Bronze.

**Silver** is where Fernbridge's real engineering work happens: parsing the raw event payload into typed columns, resolving `vehicle_id` and `package_id` against reference data, deduplicating on `event_id` so a retried scan doesn't get counted twice, and conforming event types (`scan_pickup`, `scan_in_transit`, `scan_delivered`, `gps_ping`) to one consistent set of values. **Gold** is the governance layer -- `package_status_gold` is the single place "current status" is ever calculated, derived by taking the latest Silver event per `package_id`, ordered by the event's own timestamp rather than by when Databricks happened to process it, and `delivery_performance_gold` rolls that same governed status up into the daily on-time and exception metrics operations actually reports on. If a number ever needs recalculating, there should be exactly one place to look, not three.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- Write the grain statement for each layer before anything else

The same discipline a star-schema project applies to a fact table applies here, once per layer:

```
BRONZE grain: one row = one raw Kafka message from fernbridge.delivery-events,
              exactly as produced, never updated or deleted.

SILVER grain: one row = one deduplicated, typed, conformed delivery event
              (one scan or GPS ping), keyed by event_id.

GOLD grain (package_status_gold):      one row per package_id, its CURRENT status.
GOLD grain (delivery_performance_gold): one row per vehicle, per calendar day.
```

## Step 2 -- Assign one job per layer, and write down what each is NOT allowed to do

```
LAYER    JOB                                       NOT ALLOWED TO DO
Bronze   Append-only landing of the raw Kafka       Dedup, type casting beyond
         event, with Kafka metadata preserved        raw bytes, dropping any row
Silver   Parse, type, dedup on event_id,             Deciding current package
         conform event_type values                   status -- that's Gold's job
Gold     The one governed answer: current            New raw parsing logic --
         status per package, daily performance        Gold assembles, it doesn't
         aggregates                                    reinterpret raw events
```

## Step 3 -- Name the Unity Catalog three-level namespace now, for every later lesson to reuse

```
Catalog: fernbridge          (one catalog per environment: fernbridge, fernbridge_dev)
Schemas: bronze, silver, gold

fernbridge.bronze.raw_delivery_events
fernbridge.silver.delivery_events_clean
fernbridge.gold.package_status_gold
fernbridge.gold.delivery_performance_gold
```

## Step 4 -- Whiteboard the Bronze table

```sql
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS fernbridge.bronze.raw_delivery_events (
    kafka_topic       STRING,
    kafka_partition   INT,
    kafka_offset      BIGINT,
    kafka_timestamp   TIMESTAMP,
    event_key         STRING,      -- the Kafka message key (vehicle_id)
    raw_payload       STRING,      -- the untouched JSON/Avro payload, as text
    kafka_ingest_timestamp      TIMESTAMP
)
USING DELTA
LOCATION 'abfss://bronze@fernbridgedlsprod.dfs.core.windows.net/raw_delivery_events';
```

Every column here describes the message, not the business. `raw_payload` is stored whole, unparsed -- parsing happens one layer up, deliberately, so a malformed payload lands successfully in Bronze instead of being silently dropped by a Structured Streaming job at 2am.

## Step 5 -- Whiteboard the Silver table and the dedup key

```sql
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS fernbridge.silver.delivery_events_clean (
    event_id          STRING NOT NULL,   -- dedup key
    vehicle_id        STRING NOT NULL,
    package_id        STRING NOT NULL,
    event_type        STRING NOT NULL,   -- scan_pickup | scan_in_transit |
                                          -- scan_delivered | gps_ping
    event_timestamp   TIMESTAMP NOT NULL, -- when the scan/ping actually happened
    scanner_id        STRING,
    gps_lat           DOUBLE,
    gps_lon           DOUBLE,
    _silver_loaded_at TIMESTAMP
)
USING DELTA
LOCATION 'abfss://silver@fernbridgedlsprod.dfs.core.windows.net/delivery_events_clean';
```

The dedup rule being whiteboarded here -- drop duplicate rows by `event_id` -- is simple, correct for the case it's built for (a scanner's network retry resending the identical event), and worth remembering by name, because it is also exactly the rule a later lesson in this series finds a real gap in once out-of-order delivery enters the picture.

## Step 6 -- Whiteboard the two Gold tables

```sql
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS fernbridge.gold.package_status_gold (
    package_id         STRING NOT NULL,
    current_status      STRING NOT NULL,  -- picked_up | in_transit |
                                           -- out_for_delivery | delivered | exception
    status_event_time   TIMESTAMP NOT NULL, -- the governing event's own timestamp
    last_vehicle_id      STRING,
    last_known_lat       DOUBLE,
    last_known_lon       DOUBLE,
    _gold_refreshed_at   TIMESTAMP
)
USING DELTA
LOCATION 'abfss://gold@fernbridgedlsprod.dfs.core.windows.net/package_status_gold';

CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS fernbridge.gold.delivery_performance_gold (
    delivery_date         DATE NOT NULL,
    vehicle_id             STRING NOT NULL,
    packages_delivered      INT,
    on_time_delivery_rate    DOUBLE,
    avg_transit_hours        DOUBLE,
    exception_count          INT
)
USING DELTA
LOCATION 'abfss://gold@fernbridgedlsprod.dfs.core.windows.net/delivery_performance_gold';
```

`package_status_gold` is deliberately keyed by `status_event_time`, not by whatever time Databricks happened to process the row -- "current" has to mean "most recent real-world event," not "most recently seen by the job," or the whole point of building a governed status table is lost the first night two events arrive out of order.

## Step 7 -- Draw it as an actual funnel and check it against Step 1

Bronze (one wide, append-only table) narrows into Silver (one clean, deduplicated event table) and narrows again into two Gold tables built for two different questions -- "where is this package" and "how did this vehicle perform today." If any later lesson wants to add business logic directly into Bronze, or wants Power BI or the Fabric Eventhouse to query Silver directly, that's the signal to come back to this whiteboard before writing the code.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Whiteboarded the medallion layering before touching Databricks. Bronze stays append-only and immutable -- raw Kafka events, untouched, in fernbridge.bronze.raw_delivery_events. Silver parses, types, and dedups on event_id into fernbridge.silver.delivery_events_clean. Gold is the only governed layer -- package_status_gold defines current status once, keyed by the event's own timestamp, and delivery_performance_gold rolls that up daily. That boundary is what keeps 'where's my package' from ever having two different answers again.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: We've mapped out exactly how scan and GPS data will move through the platform before any table gets built -- a raw landing zone, a cleanup layer, and one final set of tables everyone actually queries. This is the step that guarantees support and operations are looking at the same package status, not two different numbers built in the same system.
workplaceExplanation.executive: We designed exactly how incoming scan and GPS data gets captured, cleaned, and turned into one trusted package-status answer -- before building anything. That's the structural fix for 'where's my package,' not a patch on top of the manual process you have today.

lessons.title: Planning Infrastructure as Code: Terraform and Bicep Before Any Resource Exists
lessons.summary: Deciding the Terraform/Bicep split and the Git branch-and-PR workflow infra changes go through -- before a single Azure resource exists.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
The medallion layering from the last video defines what the data looks like at rest. Before any of it can exist, something has to provision the actual Azure resources underneath it -- a resource group, a storage account, networking, a Databricks workspace, a Fabric capacity -- and this video plans exactly how, in code, version-controlled in Git, rather than clicked together by hand in the Azure portal. We're splitting that work between Terraform and Bicep, deciding which tool owns which resources and why, and planning the same kind of branch-and-pull-request workflow around infrastructure changes that any other code change at Fernbridge would go through.

This is the plan that lesson 8 turns into a real `terraform apply` and a real Bicep deployment. Every resource name decided here -- the resource group, the storage account, the Databricks workspace -- is the exact name every later lesson in this series, and every other agent writing the rest of this build, will reuse.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine two different construction crews building one house. One crew pours the foundation, runs the plumbing, and puts up the walls -- the stuff that almost never changes once it's built. A second crew comes in afterward to install the smart-home system, the security cameras, and the appliances -- stuff that gets upgraded and reconfigured much more often. You wouldn't want either crew improvising without a blueprint, and you definitely wouldn't want someone walking in and knocking out a wall without anyone else on the project knowing.

That's exactly what we're setting up here. One tool (Bicep) builds Fernbridge's foundation -- storage and networking. A second tool (Terraform) builds the systems on top of it -- the Databricks and Fabric workspaces. And just like a real construction project, every change to either one has to go through a written plan that someone else checks before it's allowed to happen.
lessons.explainProfessional:
This is Infrastructure as Code, and the decision that matters most here is the division of responsibility between the two tools, made explicit before either one writes a single resource. **Bicep** owns Fernbridge's foundational, rarely-changing Azure landing-zone resources -- the resource group, the VNet and subnets, the ADLS Gen2 storage account and its Bronze/Silver/Gold containers, and the Key Vault -- because these are pure Azure-native resources, ARM is the first-party deployment model for them, and Bicep's tight coupling to Azure Policy and management-group governance matters for infrastructure this foundational. **Terraform** owns the Databricks workspace, Unity Catalog metastore and catalog/schema assignment, Databricks clusters and jobs, the Microsoft Fabric capacity and workspace, and the Kafka topic configuration -- because Terraform's Databricks and Kafka providers are the mature, first-party way to manage those APIs, and because a team running infrastructure across more than just Azure benefits from one state model instead of two.

The other decision is procedural, not technical: infrastructure changes go through exactly the same Git branch, pull request, and CI review as application code, with one difference -- a branch-protection rule requiring the automated `terraform plan` or Bicep what-if output to be posted and read by a human reviewer before approval, since an infra change's blast radius is often larger than a code change's. Nobody runs `terraform apply` or `az deployment group create` from a laptop against Fernbridge's real subscription outside of CI -- the pipeline is the only thing with that credential, which is what makes "who changed production infra, and when" always answerable from `git log` instead of from memory.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- Split responsibility between the two tools, in writing, before naming a resource

```
BICEP (Azure-native, foundational, rarely changes):
  - Resource group
  - Virtual network + subnets (including the delegated subnets
    Azure Databricks requires for VNet injection)
  - ADLS Gen2 storage account + bronze/silver/gold containers
  - Key Vault

TERRAFORM (workspace-layer, changes more often, cross-provider):
  - Azure Databricks workspace resource
  - Unity Catalog metastore assignment, catalog, schemas
  - Databricks clusters, jobs, Structured Streaming job definitions
  - Microsoft Fabric capacity + workspace
  - Kafka topic (fernbridge.delivery-events) configuration
```

## Step 2 -- Lay out the two repositories side by side

```
infra/
  bicep/
    main.bicep
    modules/
      network.bicep
      storage.bicep
      keyvault.bicep
    params/
      prod.bicepparam
  terraform/
    envs/
      prod/
        main.tf
        variables.tf
        backend.tf
    modules/
      databricks-workspace/
      unity-catalog/
      fabric-capacity/
      kafka-topics/
```

## Step 3 -- Decide the Terraform backend before writing a resource block

```hcl
# infra/terraform/envs/prod/backend.tf
terraform {
  backend "azurerm" {
    resource_group_name  = "rg-fernbridge-tfstate"
    storage_account_name = "fernbridgetfstate"
    container_name       = "tfstate"
    key                  = "fernbridge-prod.tfstate"
  }
}
```

Remote state in its own storage account, separate from the data lake itself, so a mistake in the data platform's storage account can never touch the state file that describes it.

## Step 4 -- Decide the Git branching rule for infra specifically

```
main                        -- always deployable, never committed to directly
infra/<short-description>   -- one branch per infrastructure change

Examples:
  infra/add-databricks-workspace
  infra/add-delivery-events-kafka-topic
  infra/widen-silver-container-retention
```

## Step 5 -- Write the CI checks that gate every infra pull request

```yaml
# .github/workflows/infra_ci.yml
name: Infra CI
on:
  pull_request:
    paths: ["infra/**"]
jobs:
  bicep:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: az bicep build --file infra/bicep/main.bicep
      - run: az deployment group what-if \
          --resource-group rg-fernbridge-data-prod \
          --template-file infra/bicep/main.bicep \
          --parameters infra/bicep/params/prod.bicepparam
  terraform:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    defaults:
      run: { working-directory: infra/terraform/envs/prod }
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: hashicorp/setup-terraform@v3
      - run: terraform fmt -check -recursive
      - run: terraform init
      - run: terraform validate
      - run: terraform plan -out=tfplan
```

Both jobs authenticate to Azure via OIDC federated credentials, not a stored client secret -- there is no long-lived Azure credential sitting in GitHub Actions secrets for either tool.

## Step 6 -- Set branch protection so the plan has to be read, not just produced

```
BRANCH PROTECTION on main (infra/** paths):
  - Require a pull request, 2 approving reviews (not 1 -- infra's
    blast radius is wider than one application code change)
  - Require "bicep" and "terraform" checks to pass
  - Require the terraform plan / bicep what-if output to be posted
    as a PR comment before merge is allowed
  - terraform apply and az deployment group create only ever run
    from the CD pipeline on main, never from a laptop
```

## Step 7 -- Write down what CI does NOT replace

```
CI catches: invalid HCL/Bicep, a plan that fails to generate, drift
between state and reality. CI does NOT catch: "should this subnet
actually be this size," "does this Databricks workspace need this
SKU." Those are still human review questions -- which is why the
two-reviewer rule stays mandatory even with CI green.
```

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Split infra ownership before writing a resource: Bicep owns the foundational Azure landing zone -- resource group, VNet, storage, Key Vault -- and Terraform owns the Databricks workspace, Unity Catalog, Fabric capacity, and the Kafka topic. Both go through the same branch-and-PR workflow as application code, with a two-reviewer rule and a required terraform plan / Bicep what-if posted before merge, and apply only ever runs from CI, never a laptop.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: We've planned exactly how every piece of Fernbridge's cloud infrastructure gets built and reviewed before any of it exists -- version-controlled, reviewed by two people, and tested automatically on every change. That's what keeps a mistake in the infrastructure from becoming an outage nobody can trace.
workplaceExplanation.executive: Before we spin up a single cloud resource, we've planned the exact process that keeps changes to your infrastructure safe and reviewed, the same way we'd review a change to the application itself. Nothing gets built or changed by one person clicking around in a portal.

lessons.title: Planning the Real-Time Ingestion Path: Scan Events Through Kafka
lessons.summary: Topic design, partitioning by vehicle, two independent consumer groups, and real latency targets -- before a single scanner event flows through Kafka.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
The medallion layers and the Terraform/Bicep split are both planned, but neither one has anything flowing into it yet. This video plans the path a scan or GPS event actually takes from one of Fernbridge's 200 handheld scanners to the `fernbridge.delivery-events` Kafka topic, and from there to two independent consumers: the Databricks Structured Streaming job that lands Bronze, and the Fabric Eventstream feeding the real-time Eventhouse support reps will look up a package on. We're deciding the topic's partition count and partition key, how many consumer groups read the topic and why they have to be independent, and a real latency/throughput target -- all on paper, before lesson 8 provisions anything.

The partitioning decision made here matters well beyond this lesson. Partitioning by `vehicle_id` is what keeps one vehicle's events in order as they move through the pipeline -- and keeping that ordering promise straight is exactly the kind of detail a later lesson in this series finds a gap in, once a duplicate "delivered" status shows up in production.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine 200 delivery drivers each calling in updates to one big phone line at a dispatch center. If everyone's calls got jumbled into one random pile, you'd have no way to tell whether a driver's "picked up the package" call came before or after their "delivered the package" call. So instead, dispatch gives each driver their own lane into the system -- all of one driver's calls always land in the same lane, in the order the driver made them, even though all 200 drivers are calling in at the same time.

And two different people get to listen to those same calls for two different reasons: one person writes everything down in the permanent logbook (that's Databricks building Bronze), and a second person keeps a quick whiteboard update for whoever answers the front desk phone (that's Fabric's real-time board). Neither one gets in the other's way, because they're each just listening in, not taking turns.
lessons.explainProfessional:
This is Kafka topic and consumer design, and the two decisions that matter most are the partition key and the consumer-group topology. Fernbridge's 200 vehicles produce a steady mix of scan events (pickup, in-transit, out-for-delivery, delivered) and GPS pings, and the single correctness property the pipeline depends on downstream is per-vehicle ordering: Silver's dedup and Gold's "most recent status" logic both assume that events for one vehicle arrive at Databricks in the order they actually happened. Kafka only guarantees ordering within a partition, not across an entire topic, so the topic is keyed on `vehicle_id` -- every event from a given vehicle always hashes to the same partition, which preserves that vehicle's event order end to end, even while 200 vehicles' events interleave across the topic as a whole.

The topic has two independent consumer groups reading it, by design, not by accident: `cg-databricks-bronze-ingest`, the Structured Streaming job that lands every event into Bronze for the historical lakehouse, and `cg-fabric-eventstream-ingest`, Fabric's Eventstream feeding the Eventhouse support reps query for a live lookup. Because they're separate consumer groups, each tracks its own offsets independently -- a slow night for the Databricks job never blocks or delays what a support rep sees in Fabric, and vice versa. Throughput planning is modest by streaming standards: roughly 200 vehicles each generating a GPS ping every 15 seconds plus occasional scans works out to a sustained average around 80-100 events/second with bursts toward 250/second at shift-change, well inside what a right-sized topic handles comfortably -- the real target isn't raw throughput, it's keeping end-to-end latency into Bronze under about 60 seconds and into the Eventhouse under about 10 seconds, since that's the gap between "near-real-time" and a support rep still seeing yesterday's status.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- Name the topic and decide the partition key first

```
Topic:         fernbridge.delivery-events
Partition key: vehicle_id
Reasoning:     Kafka only guarantees order within a partition. Keying
               on vehicle_id guarantees every event from one vehicle
               lands in the same partition, in send order -- which is
               exactly the ordering Silver's dedup and Gold's "most
               recent status" logic both depend on.
```

## Step 2 -- Size the partition count against the vehicle fleet, not against a guess

```
Fleet size:        ~200 vehicles
Partitions:        24
Reasoning:         Enough partitions to spread 200 vehicles' keys
                   across real parallelism for both consumer groups,
                   without over-partitioning a topic this size (each
                   partition still averages ~8 vehicles' worth of
                   traffic -- comfortably even, and easy to scale up
                   later if the fleet grows).
```

## Step 3 -- Plan the topic configuration

```hcl
# infra/terraform/modules/kafka-topics/main.tf
resource "kafka_topic" "delivery_events" {
  name               = "fernbridge.delivery-events"
  partitions         = 24
  replication_factor = 3

  config = {
    "retention.ms"         = "604800000"   # 7 days -- enough to
                                              # replay/reprocess Bronze
    "min.insync.replicas"  = "2"
    "cleanup.policy"       = "delete"
  }
}
```

Seven days of retention is deliberate: it's enough buffer to re-run the Databricks Bronze job from an earlier offset if a bug is found in the ingestion logic, without needing to go back to the scanners themselves.

## Step 4 -- Define the message schema and producer key

```json
{
  "event_id": "evt_8f3a1c...",
  "vehicle_id": "VEH-0147",
  "package_id": "PKG-559213",
  "event_type": "scan_delivered",
  "event_timestamp": "2026-10-23T14:02:11Z",
  "scanner_id": "SCN-0147-A",
  "gps_lat": 33.7701,
  "gps_lon": -84.3876
}
```

```
Producer key = vehicle_id ("VEH-0147") -- NOT event_id. Keying on
event_id would scatter one vehicle's events randomly across all 24
partitions, destroying the exact ordering guarantee Step 1 exists
to protect.
```

## Step 5 -- Plan the two consumer groups, and why they stay independent

```
CONSUMER GROUP                    READS FOR                    OWNED BY
cg-databricks-bronze-ingest         Bronze landing (historical)   Databricks
                                                                  Structured Streaming
cg-fabric-eventstream-ingest         Eventhouse / KQL (live        Fabric Eventstream
                                     "where's my package" lookup)
```

Two separate consumer groups means two separate, independently-tracked sets of offsets -- neither consumer can ever block, slow down, or lose data for the other, even if one falls behind during a traffic spike.

## Step 6 -- Write the latency and throughput targets down as real numbers

```
Sustained average throughput:   80-100 events/sec
Peak (shift-change) throughput:  up to 250 events/sec
Producer -> Bronze latency target:     < 60 seconds end to end
Producer -> Eventhouse latency target:  < 10 seconds end to end
```

These numbers are what the Databricks Structured Streaming trigger interval and the Fabric Eventstream configuration get tuned against once lesson 8 stands up real infrastructure -- not an arbitrary "as fast as possible," which is impossible to test against.

## Step 7 -- Decide what happens when a consumer falls behind

```
- Each consumer group's lag (messages behind the latest offset) is
  monitored independently -- cg-databricks-bronze-ingest lagging
  does not page anyone the same way cg-fabric-eventstream-ingest
  lagging does, since the Eventhouse feeds a live support lookup
  and Bronze feeds an overnight-tolerant historical load.
- 7-day retention (Step 3) is the safety net for Bronze: a consumer
  that falls behind, or needs to be rebuilt after a bug fix, can
  reset its offset and reprocess rather than losing data.
- Producers retry on a transient broker error rather than drop the
  event -- a scanner's own retry is exactly the kind of duplicate
  event the Silver dedup step (lesson 5) is built to absorb.
```

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Planned the Kafka ingestion path before standing up anything: topic fernbridge.delivery-events, 24 partitions, keyed on vehicle_id so each vehicle's events stay in order across the pipeline, replication factor 3, 7-day retention for replay. Two independent consumer groups -- cg-databricks-bronze-ingest and cg-fabric-eventstream-ingest -- so the historical lakehouse load and the live Fabric lookup never block each other. Latency targets are under 60 seconds into Bronze and under 10 seconds into the Eventhouse.

That's what lets us hold the team to something specific instead of a vague promise of 'real-time.'

lessons.title: Provisioning the Infrastructure With Terraform and Bicep
lessons.summary: Opening Terraform and the Azure CLI for real -- deploying the resource group, storage account, Databricks workspace, and Fabric capacity from the plan in the last two videos.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
Planning is done across the last three videos -- this is the first lesson where Terraform and Bicep actually run against a real Azure subscription. We're deploying the Bicep template that stands up `rg-fernbridge-data-prod`, the `fernbridgedlsprod` ADLS Gen2 storage account with its `bronze`, `silver`, and `gold` containers, and the supporting VNet and Key Vault -- then running the Terraform configuration that provisions the `dbw-fernbridge-prod` Azure Databricks workspace, assigns the Unity Catalog metastore, creates the `fernbridge` catalog with its `bronze`/`silver`/`gold` schemas, and stands up the Fabric capacity and workspace Fabric will run the Eventhouse on.

Nothing built in this lesson has any data in it yet -- that's deliberate, and it's the same sequencing every other Full-Circle series in this catalog follows: infrastructure exists and is provable before a single Kafka event, Databricks job, or Fabric pipeline is pointed at it. By the end of this video, every resource name established on the whiteboard two videos ago is a real, running thing in Azure that later lessons build on top of.

lessons.explainProfessional:
This is the first lesson where the Infrastructure-as-Code plan from the last two videos becomes real, billable Azure resources, applied through the CI pipeline built in lesson 6 -- `az deployment group create` for Bicep, `terraform apply` for Terraform, neither one run by hand against production outside that pipeline. Sequencing matters here: Bicep deploys first, because Terraform's Databricks workspace resource and Unity Catalog external locations reference the VNet and storage account Bicep creates, pulled in via a `terraform_remote_state` or `azurerm` data source rather than hardcoded resource IDs, so a later change to the storage account's name or region doesn't silently break the Terraform state that depends on it.

The other detail worth being deliberate about is that provisioning the Databricks workspace and assigning a Unity Catalog metastore are two different API calls with two different blast radii -- a workspace can exist for minutes without being attached to any catalog at all, and confirming that attachment succeeded (rather than assuming it did because `terraform apply` exited zero) is what this lesson verifies explicitly before calling the infrastructure phase done. Catalogs and schemas created here stay empty -- the actual Bronze, Silver, and Gold tables whiteboarded in lesson 5 get created against this catalog in a later implementation lesson, once a real Kafka stream exists for Databricks to read from.

lessons.title: Building the Bronze Layer: Landing Raw Scan and GPS Events
lessons.summary: A PySpark Structured Streaming job reads Fernbridge's Kafka delivery-events topic and appends every scan and GPS ping, untouched, into a Bronze Delta table.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
Scan events and GPS pings from Fernbridge's 200 delivery vehicles are already flowing into the Kafka topic `fernbridge.delivery-events`, partitioned by `vehicle_id`. Right now that data exists for a few hours at most, then Kafka ages it out. This lesson builds the first real link in the lakehouse: a PySpark Structured Streaming job running on Databricks that reads every event off that topic and writes it, completely untouched, into a Bronze Delta table, `fernbridge.bronze.raw_delivery_events`. No cleaning, no deduplication, no business logic of any kind lives in this job -- that restraint is deliberate, and it's the entire point of a Bronze layer.

By the end of this video, every scan and GPS event Fernbridge's trucks generate has a permanent, replayable home in Delta Lake, stamped with exactly when it was ingested and exactly which Kafka offset it came from. That's the raw material every later layer -- Silver's cleanup, Gold's business logic -- will be built from. If something downstream ever turns out wrong, this is the table we come back to and reprocess from, because it still holds the event exactly as the scanner or GPS tracker sent it.
lessons.explainSimple:
Picture a mailroom at a huge company. Every single envelope that arrives gets put on a photocopier first, before anyone opens it or decides what it's about. The photocopy gets a little stamp on it: the exact time it came in, and a ticket number showing where it sat in line. Only after that photocopy exists does anyone move on to actually reading the mail and deciding what to do with it.

That photocopier is what we're building in this lesson. Fernbridge's trucks send a steady stream of "I scanned a package" and "here's my GPS location" messages. Before we try to clean any of that up or make sense of it, we copy every single message exactly as it arrived into a permanent filing cabinet, with a timestamp and a ticket number stapled to each one. Nothing gets thrown away, nothing gets fixed up yet -- that happens in the next room, later.
lessons.explainProfessional:
This is the Bronze layer of a medallion architecture, built as a PySpark Structured Streaming job reading directly from Kafka. The job uses `spark.readStream.format("kafka")`, pointed at the `fernbridge.delivery-events` topic, and parses each Kafka record's binary `value` against an explicit `StructType` schema with `from_json`, since Kafka itself only guarantees bytes, not a typed contract. Two metadata columns get attached before anything is written: `kafka_ingest_timestamp`, a `current_timestamp()` captured at write time, and `_source_offset`, pulled straight from Kafka's own `offset` column -- together these make every Bronze row traceable back to the exact moment it landed and the exact position it occupied in the topic.

Writing happens with `outputMode("append")` into a Delta table, which is the correct and really the only acceptable output mode for Bronze: we are not aggregating, not upserting, not deduplicating anything here, just appending the stream of truth as it arrives. A streaming write still needs a `checkpointLocation` even at this early stage -- Spark uses it to track which Kafka offsets have already been processed so a restart doesn't silently skip or duplicate events wholesale. We're using a simple path for it in this first version; Bronze gets fully hardened -- a production checkpoint strategy, backpressure control, and schema-violation handling -- a few lessons from now, once the basic pipe is proven to work end to end.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 — Define the event schema

Scan and GPS events arrive as JSON inside the Kafka message value. Before reading anything, define the exact shape the producers (set up in an earlier lesson) are sending:

```python
from pyspark.sql.types import (
    StructType, StructField, StringType, DoubleType, TimestampType
)

delivery_event_schema = StructType([
    StructField("event_id", StringType(), nullable=False),
    StructField("vehicle_id", StringType(), nullable=False),
    StructField("driver_id", StringType(), nullable=True),
    StructField("package_id", StringType(), nullable=True),
    StructField("event_type", StringType(), nullable=False),
    StructField("event_timestamp", TimestampType(), nullable=False),
    StructField("latitude", DoubleType(), nullable=True),
    StructField("longitude", DoubleType(), nullable=True),
    StructField("status_detail", StringType(), nullable=True),
])
```

`event_type` carries values like `PICKUP_SCAN`, `IN_TRANSIT_SCAN`, `DELIVERED_SCAN`, `EXCEPTION_SCAN`, and `GPS_PING` -- GPS pings simply leave `package_id` and `status_detail` null.

## Step 2 — Read the Kafka stream

```python
kafka_bootstrap = dbutils.secrets.get(
    scope="fernbridge-kafka", key="bootstrap-servers"
)

raw_kafka_stream = (
    spark.readStream
    .format("kafka")
    .option("kafka.bootstrap.servers", kafka_bootstrap)
    .option("subscribe", "fernbridge.delivery-events")
    .option("startingOffsets", "earliest")
    .load()
)
```

Kafka connection details never get hardcoded -- they come from a Databricks secret scope, since this topic carries operational data for every vehicle in the fleet.

## Step 3 — Parse the JSON payload and attach traceability columns

```python
from pyspark.sql.functions import from_json, col, current_timestamp

parsed_events = (
    raw_kafka_stream
    .select(
        from_json(col("value").cast("string"), delivery_event_schema).alias("event"),
        col("topic").alias("_source_topic"),
        col("partition").alias("_source_partition"),
        col("offset").alias("_source_offset"),
    )
    .select("event.*", "_source_topic", "_source_partition", "_source_offset")
    .withColumn("kafka_ingest_timestamp", current_timestamp())
)
```

Nothing here filters a row, renames a business field, or resolves an ID against a reference table -- that's Silver's job. This is purely: take the bytes, give them the shape the schema promises, and record where and when they arrived.

## Step 4 — Write the stream to the Bronze Delta table, append-only

```python
bronze_query = (
    parsed_events.writeStream
    .format("delta")
    .outputMode("append")
    .option("checkpointLocation", "/tmp/fernbridge/checkpoints/bronze_raw_delivery_events")
    .trigger(processingTime="30 seconds")
    .toTable("fernbridge.bronze.raw_delivery_events")
)
```

`outputMode("append")` is the only mode that makes sense for a Bronze landing table -- every micro-batch simply adds its rows, nothing is ever updated or removed.

## Step 5 — Verify the job is actually landing events

```python
spark.sql("""
    SELECT event_type, count(*) AS event_count
    FROM fernbridge.bronze.raw_delivery_events
    GROUP BY event_type
    ORDER BY event_count DESC
""").show()
```

Confirm row counts are climbing as the stream runs, that `_source_offset` values are monotonically increasing per partition, and that `kafka_ingest_timestamp` reflects real landing times, not the original `event_timestamp` -- those two timestamps should differ by seconds to minutes, and that gap is itself useful signal for later lessons.

## Step 6 — Check the streaming query's own progress metrics

A running Structured Streaming query exposes its own health information, which is worth looking at before trusting any downstream count:

```python
print(bronze_query.lastProgress)
print(bronze_query.status)
```

`lastProgress` reports how many input rows the most recent micro-batch processed and how long it took -- useful for noticing early if the job is falling behind the rate events actually arrive at, long before anyone downstream would notice a gap.

## Step 7 — Write down what this job deliberately does not do yet

No `dropDuplicates`, no joins to `fernbridge.reference.vehicles` or `drivers`, no filtering of malformed rows, and a checkpoint path that is not yet production-hardened. All four of those arrive in the next two lessons -- Silver's cleanup and dedup, and the later hardening pass on this exact streaming job. That ordering is deliberate: it's much easier to verify a simple append-only job works end to end first, and only then layer cleanup, resolution, and production hardening on top of a foundation that's already proven to land real events correctly.

No cleaning or dedup happens here by design -- this table is the permanent, replayable record of exactly what the fleet sent.

This is intentionally the simplest possible version of the job -- no cleanup logic yet -- so we have a proven, working raw feed before building anything that depends on it.

This raw record is what lets us rebuild or audit any later report from the original source data, not just trust whatever number a dashboard happens to show.

lessons.title: Building the Silver Layer: Cleaning and Conforming Delivery Events
lessons.summary: Deduplicating events by event ID, resolving vehicle/driver/package IDs against reference tables, and writing clean, conformed events to Silver.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
