```sql
-- Run against the Gold table directly and compare to the report card
SELECT route_id, COUNT(*) AS packages_delivered
FROM package_status_gold
WHERE current_status = 'DELIVERED'
GROUP BY route_id
ORDER BY route_id;
```

If the DAX card and this query disagree for the same route, stop before publishing -- a relationship direction or an unintended filter is altering the number, and that gets fixed now, not after Operations starts trusting it.

## Step 5 -- Confirm the Eventhouse feed is genuinely live, not just connected

Open the KQL Queryset against the `fernbridge_rt` Eventhouse built in Lesson 14 and call its own `LatestPackageStatus()` function for a package currently out for delivery, the same way Lesson 15's investigation did:

```kql
DeliveryEventsRT
| where package_id == "PKG-558214"
| invoke LatestPackageStatus()
```

Note the `event_timestamp` returned, wait roughly three minutes, and run it again. A genuinely live feed shows either a newer event for the same package or an unchanged-but-current result; a feed that's silently stalled shows the exact same row with a growing gap between `event_timestamp` and the current time -- that gap, not the Fabric portal's "connected" indicator, is the real test.

## Step 6 -- Check the two-minute requirement with a live event

Find a vehicle actively running a route, note the time a scan event fires at the handheld scanner (or in the Kafka topic, if watching the stream directly), and time how long it takes to appear in the KQL query result. This is the actual acceptance test for Lesson 2's written requirement -- not a load test, just a stopwatch and one real event, which is usually enough to catch whether the path is meaningfully under two minutes or not.

## Step 7 -- Write down the boundary for whoever opens Fabric next

```
FABRIC WORKSPACE -- TWO SURFACES, NOT ONE
  Report: "Fernbridge Operations Trends" -> Gold Delta tables, Import mode
  Eventhouse: "Fernbridge Live Status" -> fernbridge_rt.DeliveryEventsRT,
              fed directly by its own Kafka Eventstream, queried via KQL
  These do not share a dataset, a refresh schedule, or a visual. If a
  future request asks to "just add" a live field to the trend report
  or a historical trend to the live lookup, that's a new scoping
  conversation, not a quick edit.
```

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Connected a Fabric Power BI-style report to package_status_gold and delivery_performance_gold in Import mode for Operations' trend analytics, with every measure a direct read of a Gold column, validated by hand against a SQL query before publishing. Separately confirmed the Lesson 14 Eventhouse/KQL feed is genuinely live by re-running a point lookup a few minutes apart and timing a real scan event end to end -- it's landing inside the 2-minute requirement from Lesson 2. The two surfaces intentionally read from different places and don't share a dataset.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: Operations now has a trend report built on the validated historical data, and we've confirmed -- not assumed -- that Support's real-time status feed is actually working end to end, including timing how fast a real event shows up. These are two separate tools built for two separate jobs, which keeps us from quietly merging them into one thing that does both poorly.
workplaceExplanation.executive: Both halves of what you asked for are now connected and verified: Operations has a trend dashboard built on clean historical data, and Support has a live status lookup we've personally timed against a real delivery. We built them as two focused tools instead of one do-everything dashboard, because that's what actually serves each team well.

lessons.title: Presenting the New Real-Time Visibility to Support and Operations
lessons.summary: The real walkthrough meeting with Renata and Devon -- both surfaces shown together, and an honest explanation of the delivered-then-reverted status bug Support actually lived through (ticket #4471) before it was fixed.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
This is the meeting the real-time half of this project has been building toward: Renata's Operations team and Devon's Support team, in the same room, watching their two different surfaces work -- the trend report on Gold, and a live KQL lookup on a package currently in transit. Unlike a typical demo, this one has a specific piece of unfinished business sitting in the room with it: Support fielded real tickets, including ticket #4471 on package PKG-1048275, where a customer's "delivered" package appeared to revert to "out for delivery" -- the exact incident Lessons 15 and 16 root-caused and fixed -- and glossing over it now, in the glow of a successful demo, would be exactly the wrong instinct.

The real skill in this video isn't the demo itself -- both surfaces already work, and were verified in the previous lesson. It's walking Devon's team through specifically what happened to packages like PKG-1048275, in language that respects that they're the ones who fielded the confused customer calls it caused, and specifically what's now in place -- Gold's corrected event-time resolution and its regression test -- so they're not just told "it's fixed," they're shown why it won't silently happen again.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine a school fixed a problem where the lunch line sometimes called two different kids' names for the same tray by mistake. Before telling everyone "it's fixed now, don't worry about it," a good principal would actually explain to the lunch staff what caused the mix-up -- two signals arriving at the counter in the wrong order -- and show them the new rule that sorts signals correctly before anyone's name gets called. That's more trustworthy than just saying "trust me, it won't happen again."

That's this meeting. Support dealt with real confusion when a package that had genuinely been delivered briefly showed as "out for delivery" again on the tracking page. Instead of just saying "we fixed it," we're showing them exactly what caused it and exactly what new rule is now in place so they can actually believe it's handled.
lessons.explainProfessional:
The structural risk in any "it's fixed now" conversation is asking a team that was burned by a defect to simply take your word for it, which tends to produce polite nodding and quiet, lasting distrust of the system rather than genuine confidence. The better structure, and the one this video uses, is the same reconciliation discipline used elsewhere in this program: show the mechanism, not just the conclusion. Devon's team doesn't need the full PySpark window-function internals, but they do need the actual shape of the bug -- a handheld scanner that briefly lost signal mid-route, buffered a routine re-scan locally, and flushed it to Kafka about forty minutes late, well after the package's real, on-time delivery event had already arrived. Gold's resolution logic, before the fix, picked "current status" by whichever row had the latest Kafka arrival time (`kafka_ingest_timestamp`) rather than the latest real-world scan time (`event_timestamp`) -- so that late-arriving, chronologically-older re-scan briefly won, and the tracking page reverted from DELIVERED back to OUT_FOR_DELIVERY.

The fix itself is worth stating in the same concrete terms, because "it's fixed" is not the same claim as "here is specifically what changed." Gold's window function now orders by `event_timestamp` first, with `kafka_ingest_timestamp` demoted to a tiebreaker -- the exact distinction Lesson 2's written requirement specified from the start -- and a regression test added in Lesson 16 (`test_late_arriving_old_event_does_not_win`) fabricates that same late-arrival pattern on every CI run, wired into the same `test-pyspark-transforms` job from Lesson 13, so a future change that reintroduces this ordering mistake fails a build before it ever reaches a package a customer is calling about. Naming the regression test by name, not just asserting "we added tests," is what turns this from reassurance into evidence Devon's team can actually evaluate.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- Prepare the bug explanation before the meeting, not during it

Write the mechanism down in plain, sequential terms so it can be delivered calmly and consistently, not improvised under questions:

```
WHAT HAPPENED (ticket #4471, package PKG-1048275):
  1. A handheld scanner lost signal mid-route -- not unusual, it
     happens on rural stretches -- and a routine re-scan it generated
     at 8:30am got buffered locally instead of sending immediately.
  2. The package was genuinely delivered at 8:52am. That scan event
     reached Kafka on time, at 8:52:09am, and the customer correctly
     got a "delivered" text a moment later.
  3. The scanner then reconnected and flushed its buffered 8:30am
     re-scan -- which arrived at Kafka at 9:10:40am, nearly 40 minutes
     after the delivery event had already arrived.
  4. Before the fix, Gold's window function picked "current status"
     by whichever row had the LATEST KAFKA ARRIVAL TIME, not the
     latest real scan time -- so the late-arriving 8:30am re-scan beat
     the on-time 8:52am delivery, and the tracking page reverted from
     DELIVERED back to OUT_FOR_DELIVERY.
  5. The support desk's live KQL lookup, reading the same Kafka topic
     through its own independent path, showed DELIVERED correctly the
     entire time -- it was only the batch Gold table that was wrong,
     which is exactly what let Lesson 15 narrow the bug down so fast.
```

## Step 2 -- Open the meeting with the demo, in the order both teams will actually use it

```
1. Show Renata's trend report first: route-level on-time rates and
   exception counts on package_status_gold / delivery_performance_gold.
2. Show Devon's live lookup second: pull up a package that's
   currently out for delivery in the KQL Queryset, note the
   event_timestamp, and refresh it a few minutes later to show the
   status has moved.
3. Only after both surfaces have been seen working, address the bug
   directly -- don't bury it in the middle of the happy-path demo.
```

## Step 3 -- Name the bug directly, using the mechanism from Step 1

```
YOU:    Before we wrap up, I want to talk about ticket #4471 and the
        other reports like it. Here's exactly what caused it.
        [walk the room through the 5-step sequence above]
DEVON:  We definitely had calls where a customer said their package
        was delivered and our screen then said "out for delivery"
        again. Is that the same thing?
YOU:    Yes -- precisely this. A scanner reconnecting after a signal
        gap sent a routine, older re-scan to Kafka LATE, after the
        real delivery event had already arrived, and the system
        briefly trusted whichever event it received most recently
        instead of whichever one actually happened last on the truck.
```

## Step 4 -- Show the fix and the regression test, not just the word "fixed"

```python
# transforms/gold_package_status.py -- the corrected ordering
latest = Window.partitionBy("package_id").orderBy(
    F.col("event_timestamp").desc(),        # the scanner's own clock decides
    F.col("kafka_ingest_timestamp").desc(),  # only a tiebreaker now
)
```

```
"This is the rule now: whichever event has the latest real-world
scan timestamp wins, full stop -- never whichever one happened to
reach us most recently. And it's not just fixed once -- there's a
regression test, test_late_arriving_old_event_does_not_win, that
fabricates this exact late-arrival pattern on every single code
change, wired into our CI pipeline, and it fails the build if this
bug ever comes back. I can show you that test."
```

## Step 5 -- Answer the question Support will actually ask

```
DEVON:  How do we know this won't happen again in some new way we
        haven't seen yet?
YOU:    I can't promise no bug like this ever surfaces again -- any
        system reading from hardware in the field can hit a new edge
        case. What I can tell you is this specific failure mode is
        now covered by an automated test, and the underlying rule --
        trust event time, not arrival time -- is the same rule written
        into the requirement back when this project started, so it's
        not a patch bolted on after the fact, it's the system finally
        matching what was actually specified.
```

## Step 6 -- Close with what each team should do if something looks wrong again

Point Devon's team at the on-call runbook entry being written in the next lesson, specifically the section on telling a stale real-time feed apart from a genuinely out-of-order event -- so if a rep sees something odd, the first move is a documented check, not a guess or a direct page to you.

## Step 7 -- Get an explicit reaction, not just a quiet nod

Ask Devon directly whether the explanation and the fix address what his team experienced, and wait for an actual answer before moving on. A demo that goes well but skips this question risks leaving the exact distrust this video is designed to resolve sitting quietly in the room.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Walked Operations and Support through both consumption surfaces live, then addressed the Lesson 15/16 delivered-then-reverted bug directly with Support -- explained how a late-arriving re-scan beat Gold's arrival-order resolution in plain terms, showed the event-timestamp-based fix, and named the specific regression test (test_late_arriving_old_event_does_not_win) that now guards against a recurrence. Got explicit confirmation from Devon's team that the explanation matched what they'd experienced.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: Held the real walkthrough with both teams together, and didn't skip the uncomfortable part -- we explained exactly what caused the status mix-up Support dealt with, and exactly what's now in place to catch it if it tries to happen again. That's a stronger foundation for trust than a smooth demo that quietly avoids the thing people actually remember.
workplaceExplanation.executive: Both teams have now seen their new tools working, and we were straight with Support about the status mix-up some of them ran into personally -- what caused it, and what's now automatically checking for it on every future change. That kind of directness is what makes people actually trust a new system instead of just tolerating it.

lessons.title: Writing the Handoff Docs: Data Dictionary, Lineage, and an On-Call Runbook
lessons.summary: A plain-English data dictionary entry for Package Status, a prose lineage description covering both the batch and real-time paths, and a runbook entry for triaging a stale real-time feed.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
Both surfaces work, and both teams have seen them and trust them -- which means this platform is now exactly the kind of thing that needs to survive without you standing next to it. This video writes the three documents that make that possible: a plain-English data dictionary entry for "Package Status" that Devon's and Renata's teams can reread on their own months from now, a prose description of the full lineage -- handheld scanner and GPS tracker, through Kafka, Bronze, Silver, Gold, and out to both the batch report and the Eventhouse -- and an on-call runbook entry for the specific, inevitable 3am problem: the real-time feed looks stale, and whoever's on call needs to figure out fast whether that's the Kafka topic itself, the Fabric Eventstream reading it, or the Eventhouse/KQL layer beyond it -- and to rule out the batch Structured Streaming job, which doesn't touch this path at all.

These three documents answer three different questions, and that's deliberate. The dictionary answers "what does this status actually mean, and what's it not telling me." The lineage answers "where does this number come from, start to finish." The runbook answers the one question that actually matters at 3am: "where do I look first."
lessons.explainSimple: Imagine you build a really good treehouse, and before you hand the ladder over to the next kid, you leave three notes taped inside: one plain note explaining what the rope swing actually does and doesn't do, one note tracing exactly how water gets from the roof to the rain barrel, and one emergency note that says "if the rain barrel looks empty, check these three things in this order before you panic." That's exactly what this video writes for the data platform, instead of just walking away and hoping nobody needs to ask you anything.
lessons.explainProfessional:
A data dictionary entry earns its keep specifically on what it excludes, not on what it includes -- anyone can write "Package Status: the current status of a package," and that sentence has never once prevented a misunderstanding. A useful entry for "Package Status" states plainly that it reflects the single latest event by true event timestamp, not by arrival order, and that it does not represent a GPS-based live location -- a genuinely different thing a stakeholder might reasonably assume it means, given that GPS pings exist in this system too. Naming that boundary in writing is what stops a future analyst or a new support rep from quietly reinterpreting the field six months from now, the same drift this program has been careful to prevent at every other handoff point.

The lineage description does real work precisely by staying in prose rather than a diagram alone, because prose forces the two paths -- batch and real-time -- to be narrated as the genuinely different journeys they are, from the same two source devices, through the same Kafka topic, but diverging immediately at that topic: one path continuing through Bronze, Silver, and Gold into the Fabric report on a 15-minute batch schedule, the other read a second time, independently, straight into the Eventhouse for point lookups. The runbook entry is the most operationally valuable of the three specifically because it's structured as a decision tree rather than a list of facts -- staleness in a multi-hop pipeline can originate at any of three independent points, and an on-call engineer at 3am needs an ordered way to localize the failure, not a reference manual to read cover to cover while packages keep moving and nobody can tell where they are.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- Write the Package Status data dictionary entry

```
FIELD: Package Status (package_status_gold.current_status /
       the Eventhouse's live status result)
PLAIN-ENGLISH DEFINITION: The single most recent real-world status
       of a package, determined by the event with the latest true
       EVENT TIMESTAMP -- when the scan actually happened on the
       truck -- never by which event reached our system most recently
       (its KAFKA ARRIVAL TIME).
WHAT THIS EXCLUDES:
  - NOT a live GPS location -- the last known scan-based STATUS, not
    a map position. GPS pings exist but feed a separate concern.
  - NOT a sub-second guarantee. Real-time targets 2 minutes (Lesson
    2); batch Gold refreshes every 15 minutes and can lag by design.
  - DELIVERED means a scanner recorded a delivery scan -- not a
    customer-signature record, which lives in a separate system.
WHERE IT LIVES: package_status_gold.current_status (batch, resolved in
       transforms/gold_package_status.py) and the fernbridge_rt
       Eventhouse's DeliveryEventsRT table via LatestPackageStatus()
       (real-time). Both resolve "latest" by event_timestamp -- the
       Eventhouse always did, via KQL's arg_max(); Gold was corrected
       to match in Lessons 15-16.
LAST CHANGED: Lessons 15-16, when Gold's window function was corrected
       to order by event_timestamp instead of kafka_ingest_timestamp
       (arrival order), fixing the delivered-then-reverted incident on
       ticket #4471.
OWNER: Data Engineering. Changing this definition requires sign-off
       from both Operations and Support, since both surfaces depend
       on the same rule.
```

## Step 2 -- Write the lineage description in prose, covering both paths

```
LINEAGE -- FERNBRIDGE PACKAGE STATUS

Every status starts the same way: a handheld scanner or GPS tracker on
one of roughly 200 vehicles fires an event -- a scan at pickup,
out-for-delivery, delivery, or exception, or a location ping roughly
every 45 seconds on an active route. Every event publishes to the
Kafka topic fernbridge.delivery-events, the one shared starting point
for everything downstream.

From there, the two paths diverge on purpose. In the BATCH path, Azure
Databricks Structured Streaming reads the topic and lands every event,
as-is, in Bronze -- nothing cleaned yet. A Silver job then conforms
those events: deduplicating retransmissions and resolving each
package's current status by true event timestamp, never arrival order
-- the rule the Lesson 15-16 fix hardened. From Silver, a Gold job
resolves one current status per package into package_status_gold and
rolls outcomes up to the route level in delivery_performance_gold.
Both feed a Fabric report on the orchestrated pipeline's schedule, for
Operations' trend analytics.

In the REAL-TIME path, the same Kafka topic is read a second time, independently, by a Fabric Eventstream under its own consumer group (fabric-rt-reader) -- it never touches Bronze, Silver, or Gold. It lands events straight into the fernbridge_rt Eventhouse's DeliveryEventsRT table, and the LatestPackageStatus() KQL function resolves current status by each event's own event_timestamp -- the same rule Gold now uses, arrived at independently rather than inherited from the batch path. The Eventhouse is what Support's live lookup queries against, targeting Lesson 2's 2-minute requirement.

Both paths share one source and one starting point, and since Lesson 16's fix, the same resolution rule, through two separate consumers. They diverge only in how much freshness each trades for governed, cheaply-queryable history.
```

## Step 3 -- Write the on-call runbook entry for a stale real-time feed

```
RUNBOOK: Real-Time Feed Looks Stale
(Support reports a package status that clearly hasn't updated in a
while, or a KQL query returns an old event_timestamp with no newer
rows for an actively moving package)

CHECK 1 -- Is it Kafka ingestion?
  Query the fernbridge.delivery-events topic's consumer lag directly.
  If lag is climbing with no new messages arriving at all, check the
  scanner/GPS ingestion gateway first -- likely a device or cellular
  issue upstream, not a platform bug. If messages ARE arriving: Check 2.

CHECK 2 -- Is it the Fabric Eventstream?
  Open the Eventstream in the Fabric portal and check its throughput.
  A healthy Eventstream shows a steady flow of rows landing in
  DeliveryEventsRT; a stalled one shows the gap directly. If Kafka has
  messages but DeliveryEventsRT doesn't, the issue is the Eventstream
  itself, not the topic or the Eventhouse beyond it.

CHECK 3 -- Is it the Eventhouse / KQL layer?
  Run LatestPackageStatus() for a known-active package directly
  against the Eventhouse. If DeliveryEventsRT has fresh rows but the
  function returns stale results, the issue is in the KQL function or
  the Eventhouse database itself, not upstream.

NOTE: The Bronze/Silver Structured Streaming job and the
  fernbridge_silver_to_gold Workflow feed the BATCH path only -- they
  do not touch the real-time surface at all. Don't spend time on
  either of those for a stale real-time ticket; they're a separate
  investigation if the trend report looks stale instead.

ESCALATION: If all three checks look healthy but Support still
  reports stale data, check that specific package_id's actual scan
  history -- a package stuck mid-route by a real-world delay can
  look identical to a platform problem on a rep's screen, and this
  resolves faster than re-checking the whole pipeline.
```

## Step 4 -- Store all three where the next person will actually find them

Put the data dictionary and lineage description in the same shared documentation space Operations and Support already use, not a personal notes file, and pin the runbook entry specifically where whoever is on call will look first during an incident, not buried several pages into a general wiki. Walk one person from each team through where to find each document before calling this handoff done -- a document nobody was shown how to use might as well not exist.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Wrote the Package Status data dictionary entry, explicit about what it excludes -- not a live GPS location, not a sub-second guarantee, not a proof-of-delivery record. lessons.title: Wrap-Up: What Changed, and What's Still Manual
lessons.summary: The honest closing assessment of the whole Fernbridge Logistics build -- what's genuinely solved for Operations and Support, and what's still manual, fragile, or upstream of everything built here.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
This is the last video in the series, and like the rest of this program, it isn't a highlight reel. Over nineteen lessons, Fernbridge Logistics went from a day-stale manual CSV export and a support desk with zero current-state visibility to a real Kafka event stream, a medallion lakehouse on Azure Databricks and Delta Lake with a resolved Gold layer, two purpose-built Fabric consumption surfaces, infrastructure provisioned through Terraform and Bicep and tested through Git CI, and a real delivered-then-reverted status bug that was found, root-caused, fixed, and covered by a regression test. That part is real, it's in production, and both Operations and Support are using it.

What this video does instead of celebrating is the harder, more useful thing: naming exactly what's still manual, still fragile, or still upstream of everything this program built, so whoever maintains this platform next -- possibly you, six months from now -- isn't caught off guard by a limitation that was always there but never said out loud.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine you spent weeks building a genuinely solid treehouse with strong boards, a good ladder, and a roof that doesn't leak. It's great. But a good builder doesn't just say "it's perfect, goodbye" -- they say "this part is solid, but that rope still needs checking every few months, and if the actual tree it's built on ever gets sick, that's a bigger problem no amount of treehouse repair fixes." That honesty is what makes the treehouse actually safe to keep using, instead of someone discovering its limits the hard way later, in the dark, during a storm.

That's this whole video: being straight about what's genuinely solid in what got built for Fernbridge, and what still needs a person checking in on it.
lessons.explainProfessional:
A credible project retrospective does two things most victory-lap wrap-ups skip: it states the real architecture plainly enough that someone who missed the first nineteen videos could still understand what's running, and it enumerates the actual gaps with the same specificity the earlier lessons used for the delivered-then-reverted status bug -- not "there's room for improvement," but named, concrete limitations. For Fernbridge, three are worth stating without softening. There is no automated data-quality alerting beyond what CI catches on a pull request, so a bad value or a new edge case that reaches production between deploys has no monitor watching for it until a person notices a number or a status looks wrong -- the same way the delivered-then-reverted bug on ticket #4471 was originally caught by Devon's team noticing, not by an alert firing. The real-time Eventhouse path and the batch Gold path can briefly disagree during a backfill or a stream replay, because they're intentionally two separate consumers of the same Kafka topic rather than one computed value propagated to two places -- which is the correct tradeoff for keeping each surface fast at its own job, but it means a reconciliation gap during an unusual operation, like a replay after an outage, is a real possibility, not a theoretical one. And Kafka itself, along with the roughly 200 handheld scanners and GPS trackers generating every event this entire platform depends on, remains the one upstream layer no amount of Bronze, Silver, Gold, or Fabric engineering protects -- if a scanner fails, loses signal, or a device fleet-wide firmware issue ever disrupted event generation at the source, there's nothing downstream that fixes a gap that never arrives.

Naming these isn't an admission of failure -- overselling a system's completeness to a stakeholder is itself a trust problem, the same category of problem the delivered-then-reverted incident already tested this team's honesty on once, mid-project. The honest version of "done" is "this solved the specific, real problems Renata and Devon brought to that first discovery meeting, these are its real edges, and here's what a future phase would need to address them."
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- State the finished architecture in one pass, end to end

```
SOURCE:        ~200 delivery vehicles, handheld scanner + GPS tracker each
STREAM:        Kafka topic fernbridge.delivery-events
BATCH PATH:     Azure Databricks Structured Streaming
               -> Bronze (raw, as-is) -> Silver (deduped, conformed,
                  resolved by true event timestamp) -> Gold
                  (package_status_gold, delivery_performance_gold)
               -> Fabric Power BI-style report (Operations' trends)
REAL-TIME PATH: Same Kafka topic -> Fabric Eventhouse / KQL database
               (same conformance rule as Silver) -> live lookups
                  (Support's 2-minute requirement)
ORCHESTRATED BY: A scheduled batch pipeline for the Bronze/Silver/Gold
               path, with the real-time path running continuously
INFRASTRUCTURE:  Provisioned via Terraform and Bicep
TESTED BY:     Git CI -- notebook tests, infra validation, and a
               regression test for the Lesson 15-16 out-of-order
               event bug specifically
```

Every box in that chain was built, tested, and is now genuinely in use by both Operations and Support -- that's the real, defensible claim this project gets to make.

## Step 2 -- Name what's still manual or fragile, specifically

```
GAP 1: No automated data-quality alerting beyond CI.
  CI tests only run when a pull request triggers them. A bad value or
  a new edge case that reaches production between deploys -- a new
  kind of scanner firmware quirk, an unusual Kafka replay -- has no
  monitor watching live production data until a person notices.
  That's exactly how the original delivered-then-reverted status on
  ticket #4471 was found: Devon's team noticed, not an alert.

GAP 2: Batch Gold and the real-time Eventhouse can briefly disagree.
  They're two independent consumers of the same Kafka topic, by
  design, so each stays fast at its own job -- but that also means
  during a backfill or a stream replay after an outage, the two
  surfaces can show a package at slightly different states for a
  short window before both catch up. This is a known tradeoff of the
  architecture, not a bug, but it's worth saying out loud rather than
  letting someone discover it mid-incident.

GAP 3: Kafka and the scanner/GPS fleet are the true single points of
  failure.
  Every Bronze, Silver, Gold, and Fabric component in this platform
  depends on events actually arriving at the Kafka topic in the first
  place. No amount of downstream engineering protects against a
  scanner failing, losing signal for an extended period, or a
  fleet-wide device issue -- it protects everything built on top of
  the event stream, not the devices and stream generating it.
```

## Step 3 -- Write the honest one-paragraph summary for whoever reads this next

```
"This project replaced a day-stale manual CSV export and a support
desk with zero current-state visibility with a real Kafka-to-lakehouse
platform that both Operations and Support now genuinely use, and it
found and fixed a real out-of-order event bug along the way, with a
regression test guarding against its return. It did not add production
alerting beyond CI, a way to guarantee the batch and real-time paths
never diverge during an unusual replay, or any protection for the
scanner/GPS fleet and Kafka itself going down -- those are real, named
gaps for a future phase, not oversights we're pretending don't exist."
```

## Step 4 -- Leave a short, prioritized list for "if there's a phase two"

```
1. Production data-quality monitoring independent of CI, with
   alerting on the live pipeline -- closes Gap 1, highest value for
   the lowest lift.
2. A documented reconciliation check comparing batch Gold and
   Eventhouse state after any backfill or replay -- closes Gap 2.
3. Redundancy or health-monitoring for the scanner/GPS fleet and
   Kafka's own availability -- closes Gap 3, hardest and most
   expensive, and the one that would need Fernbridge's hardware
   vendor at the table, not just this data team.
```

## Step 5 -- Close the series the way it opened: with the two people who started it

The first video in this series was a discovery meeting with Renata and Devon, two stakeholders describing what turned out to be two different problems. It's worth closing on the same note: both of their problems got solved, specifically and verifiably, and both of them know exactly what this platform does and doesn't cover going forward -- which is a more durable ending than a demo that looked impressive in the room and quietly oversold what's actually there.

Named three real gaps rather than glossing over them: no production alerting beyond CI, a possible batch/real-time reconciliation gap during a backfill or replay, and the scanner/GPS fleet plus Kafka itself remaining the true upstream single point of failure.
